entry: [[Naval warfare]] force of the [[United Kingdom]], responsible for defending the country from naval attack or invasion. Its origins lie in the English Navy of the early 16th century, making it the oldest of the United Kingdom's armed services. From the early 18th century until World War II it was the world's most powerful navy, and it helped defend the [[British Empire]]. During the [[Cold War]] it became chiefly an anti-submarine force; after the collapse of the [[Soviet Union]] its focus returned to expeditionary operations. As of July 2026 it had 60 active and commissioned ships, including [[Submarine|submarines]].

American drag queen and television host. He achieved international fame with the 1993 single "Supermodel (You Better Work)." He produces, hosts and judges the reality competition series RuPaul's Drag Race, which was created in 2009 and has produced 18 seasons in the United States. He has received 14 Primetime Emmy Awards and a Tony Award, and in 2018 he received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]]. He has released 15 studio albums and published four books. He created and starred in the [[Netflix]] original series AJ and the Queen (2020).

English translation of Persian quatrains attributed to [[Omar Khayyam]], dubbed "the Astronomer-Poet of Persia." Edward FitzGerald's 1859 translation, drawn from two Persian manuscripts, was commercially unsuccessful at first. It was popularized from 1861 by Whitley Stokes and admired by the Pre-Raphaelites in England. A third edition in 1872 increased interest in the [[United States]], and by the 1880s the work was extremely popular, inspiring numerous "Omar Khayyam clubs." It has been published in several hundred editions. Scholars regard the authenticity of the verses attributed to Khayyam as highly uncertain, because the earliest reference to him writing poetry appears 43 years after his death.

Viral infection, also known as German measles or three-day measles, caused by the rubella virus. Symptoms are often mild. A rash, usually starting on the face, lasts three days, and fever, swollen lymph nodes and joint pain may also occur. The virus spreads through the air in coughs, and people are infectious for about a week before and after the rash. Infection in early [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]] may cause miscarriage or congenital rubella syndrome, which can affect the eyes, hearing, [[Heart|heart]] and brain. A single dose of the [[Vaccine|vaccine]] is more than 95% effective, and it is often given as the combined [[Measles|measles]], mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. There is no specific treatment. The name comes from the Latin for "little red." In April 2015 the [[World Health Organization]] declared the [[Americas]] free of rubella transmission.

Family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] commonly known as the [[Coffee|coffee]], madder or bedstraw family. It contains about 14,200 [[Species|species]] in about 615 genera, making it the fourth-largest angiosperm family by number of species. It has a cosmopolitan distribution, but the greatest diversity is in the [[Tropics|tropics]] and subtropics. Members include [[Shrub|shrubs]], [[Tree|trees]], lianas and herbs, with simple, opposite leaves and interpetiolar stipules. Economically important genera include Coffea, the source of coffee; Cinchona, the source of the antimalarial [[Quinine|quinine]]; and ornamentals such as [[Gardenia]], Ixora and Pentas. Some dye plants, such as Rubia, have historically been used. Fruits are berries, capsules, drupes or schizocarps, and red fruits are fairly common.

[[Chemical element]] with symbol Rb and atomic number 37. It is a very soft, whitish-gray solid [[Alkali metal|alkali metal]] similar to [[Potassium]] and [[Caesium|cesium]]. It is the first alkali metal in its group with a density higher than water, and it reacts explosively with water to produce rubidium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. German chemists Robert Bunsen and [[Gustav Kirchhoff]] discovered it in 1861 by flame spectroscopy. The name comes from the Latin *rubidus*, meaning deep red, the color of its emission spectrum. Natural rubidium is 72% stable [[Isotope|isotope]] ⁸⁵Rb and 28% slightly radioactive ⁸⁷Rb, with a [[Half-life|half-life]] of 48.8 billion years. Rubidium chloride is used to induce living cells to take up [[DNA]].

Three-dimensional combination puzzle invented in 1974 by [[Hungary|Hungarian]] sculptor and architecture professor Ernő Rubik. Originally called the Magic Cube, it was licensed to Ideal Toy Corp and released internationally in 1980, when it won the German Game of the Year special award for Best Puzzle. As of January 2024, around 500 million cubes had been sold, making it the world's bestselling puzzle game and bestselling toy. On the classic version each of the six faces has nine stickers, and since 1988 the colors have been standardized, with white opposite yellow, blue opposite green and orange opposite red. An internal pivot mechanism lets each layer turn independently. The cube was inducted into the US National Toy Hall of Fame in 2014. Since 2003 the World Cube Association has organized competitions and recognized world records.

Red variety of the mineral [[Corundum]], used as a [[Gemstone|gemstone]]. Rubies range from pinkish-red to blood-red and have a hardness of 9.0 on the [[Mohs scale]]. Their color comes from [[Chromium|chromium]], and ruby is one of the traditional cardinal gems, alongside amethyst, sapphire, emerald and diamond. The name comes from the Latin word for red. Some gems historically called rubies, such as the Black Prince's Ruby in the British Imperial State Crown, are actually [[Spinel|spinels]]. The most valued shade, blood-red or pigeon blood, commands a large premium. The world's most valuable ruby sold at auction was the Estrela de Fura, which sold for US$34.8 million.

General-purpose programming language designed with an emphasis on productivity and simplicity. In Ruby, everything is an object, including primitive data types. Development began in the mid-1990s by Yukihiro "Matz" Matsumoto in Japan, and the first public release, Ruby 0.95, was announced in December 1995. Ruby is interpreted, high-level and dynamically typed, and it supports procedural, [[Object-oriented programming|object-oriented]] and [[Functional programming|functional]] paradigms. According to its creator, it was influenced by Perl, Smalltalk, Eiffel, Ada, BASIC and [[Lisp (programming language)|Lisp]].

Persian poet, singer and musician regarded as the first major poet to write in New Persian. A court poet under the Samanids, he was based mainly at Bukhara, and his primary patron was the vizier Abu'l-Fadl al-Bal'ami. He was also known for his fine voice and his playing of the *chang*. Only a small portion of his work survives, most notably parts of his versification of the *Kalila wa-Dimna*, an Arabic translation of the [[Panchatantra]]. After Bal'ami fell in 937, Rudaki's career declined, and he was dismissed from court. He spent his last years in poverty, dying blind and alone in his hometown. In [[Iran]] he is acknowledged as the "founder of New Persian poetry," and in [[Tajikistan]] as the "father of Tajik literature."

Extinct order of marine bivalve mollusks, shaped like boxes, tubes or rings. They arose in the Late [[Jurassic]] and became so diverse in the [[Cretaceous]] that they were major reef builders in the [[Tethys Ocean]]. In reef-building forms, one valve became a flat lid and the other an inverted, spike-like cone whose size ranged from a few centimeters to well over a meter in length. The oldest true rudists are found in Late Jurassic rocks in France. They became extinct at the end of the Cretaceous, apparently as a result of the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]].

German mechanical engineer and inventor, best known for the [[Diesel engine]], which burns [[Diesel fuel|diesel fuel]]; both are named for him. He trained at the Royal Bavarian Polytechnic of Munich, where one of his professors was the engineer Carl von Linde. Diesel worked on refrigeration plants with Linde in Paris and later managed Linde's research and development department in Berlin. During tests of a [[Steam engine|steam engine]] that used ammonia vapor, the engine exploded and almost killed him, and he began conceptualizing the diesel engine during this period. His family had been deported to England at the outbreak of the [[Franco-Prussian War]].

German SS officer and longest-serving commandant of [[Auschwitz concentration camp|Auschwitz]], from 1940 to 1943 and again from 1944 to 1945. He implemented methods for the [[Final Solution]], introducing the pesticide Zyklon B into gas chambers, where over a million people were killed. After the war he lived under a false name until British forces discovered him. Handed over to Polish authorities, he was convicted of [[War crime|war crimes]] and executed. While imprisoned he wrote memoirs, published in English as *Commandant of Auschwitz: The Autobiography of Rudolf Hoess*.

German Nazi politician and deputy to [[Adolf Hitler]], holding that position from 1933 to 1941. He assisted Hitler with *Mein Kampf* during his imprisonment after the [[Beer Hall Putsch]]. On 10 May 1941 he flew solo to [[Scotland]] in an attempt to negotiate the [[United Kingdom]]'s exit from the [[World War II|Second World War]]. British authorities arrested him, and at the 1946 [[Nuremberg trials]] he was convicted of crimes against peace and conspiracy. He served a life sentence in Spandau Prison, where the [[Soviet Union]] blocked repeated attempts to win his release.

Soviet-born ballet dancer and choreographer, widely regarded as the preeminent male ballet dancer of the 20th century. He was born on a Trans-Siberian train near [[Lake Baikal]] and began his career in Leningrad with the company then called the Kirov Ballet. In 1961 he defected to the West despite efforts by the [[KGB]], the first defection of a Soviet artist during the [[Cold War]]. He danced with The Royal Ballet in London and became a global star, helping to elevate the role of the male dancer in ballet. From 1983 to 1989 he directed the Paris Opera Ballet as its chief choreographer. He also produced his own interpretations of classics, including *Swan Lake*, *Giselle* and *La Bayadère*.

German physician and polymath, known as the "father of modern [[Pathology|pathology]]." His investigation of the 1847–1848 [[Typhus|typhus]] epidemic in Upper Silesia laid the foundation for [[Public health|public health]] in Germany. His book *Cellular Pathology* (1858) is regarded as the root of modern pathology. He was the first to describe and name diseases such as [[Leukemia|leukemia]], and he developed the first systematic method of [[Autopsy|autopsy]]. A co-founder of the Deutsche Fortschrittspartei, he opposed [[Otto von Bismarck]]'s financial policy but supported Bismarck's anti-Catholic campaigns, which he named *Kulturkampf*. He opposed germ theory and rejected [[Ignaz Semmelweis]]'s idea of disinfecting. He produced more than 2,000 scientific writings.

[[Italy|Italian]]-born actor and dancer, dubbed the "Latin Lover." He began as a taxi dancer and later moved into ballroom dancing before becoming one of the most iconic stars of American [[Silent film|silent cinema]]. His breakthrough came with *The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse* (1921), which popularized the Argentine [[Tango|tango]] with American audiences. He went on to star in *The Sheik* (1921), *Blood and Sand* (1922), *The Eagle* (1925) and *The Son of the Sheik* (1926). His screen image made him the first [[Sex symbol|sex symbol]], provoking both fervent adoration and cultural backlash. In 1925 he established the Rudolph Valentino Medal, a precursor to the Academy Award.

English journalist, novelist, poet and [[Short story|short-story]] writer. He was born in British India, which inspired much of his work. His fiction includes *The Jungle Book* (1894), *Kim* (1901) and *Just So Stories* (1902), and his poems include "Mandalay" and "Gunga Din." In 1907 he received the Nobel Prize in [[Literature]], the first English-language recipient and, at age 41, the youngest to date. He declined the British Poet Laureateship and several offers of a knighthood. [[Henry James]] called him "the most complete man of genius" he had known. The critic Douglas Kerr described him as "an incomparable, if controversial, interpreter of how empire was experienced." His ashes were interred at Poets' Corner in [[Westminster Abbey]].

International [[Rugby league]] tournament contested by senior men's national teams. The first tournament was held in France in 1954, the first world cup held for any form of [[Rugby football|rugby football]]. It is now played every four years, with a group and knockout structure. The winners receive the Paul Barrière Trophy, named after the French Rugby League president of the 1940s and 1950s. Australia is the most successful team, while Great Britain has won three titles and New Zealand one. The 2026 edition was held in Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea.

International men's [[Rugby union|rugby union]] competition, contested every four years between the top international teams. World Rugby administers it, and the winners receive the Webb Ellis Cup, named after William Webb Ellis, who according to legend invented rugby by picking up the ball. The first tournament was held in 1987, co-hosted by New Zealand and Australia. South Africa has won four times, New Zealand three times, Australia twice and England once, and South Africa won the 2023 final against New Zealand. Sixteen teams took part from 1987 to 1995, and the field expanded to 20 in 1999 and will expand to 24 for the 2027 tournament in Australia. [[Japan]] hosted the 2019 tournament and France hosted in 2023.

Family of team sports comprising [[Rugby union|rugby union]] and [[Rugby league|rugby league]]. Rugby football began at Rugby School in Rugby, Warwickshire, England, where its rules were first written down in 1845. It spread through English public schools and across the [[British Empire]] in the 19th century. In 1895 northern English clubs broke away from the Rugby Football Union over payments to players, and rugby league became the first football code to pay players. Rugby union allowed professional players in 1995. The first rules of the Melbourne Football Club, which became [[Australian rules football]], were devised from players' experiences of rugby football in 1859.

Full-contact sport played by two teams of 13 players on a rectangular field. It originated in 1895 in Huddersfield, in [[Yorkshire|West Yorkshire]], England, as a breakaway from the Rugby Football Union over payments to players. Its rules were changed to produce a faster and more entertaining game for paying spectators. It is one of two codes of [[Rugby football|rugby football]], the other being [[Rugby union]]. A try is worth four points, and conversions and penalties are worth two each, while a drop goal is worth one. The sport is played mainly by [[Australasia|Australasian]], [[Europe|European]] and Pacific Island countries, and it is the national sport of [[Papua New Guinea]] and the [[Cook Islands]]. The first [[Rugby League World Cup]] was held in France in 1954, the first World Cup of either rugby code.

Variant of [[Rugby union|rugby union]] played by teams of seven players in two seven-minute halves. It originated in the 1880s in Melrose, a [[Scotland|Scottish]] town, and the Melrose Sevens is still played annually. The Hong Kong Sevens helped popularize the game in Asia, and the sport joined the Commonwealth Games in 1998. Rugby sevens was first contested at the Summer Olympics in 2016. Scoring follows rugby union, with five points for a try, two for a conversion and three for a penalty or drop goal. Tournaments are often completed in a day or a weekend and are known for a relaxed atmosphere.

Close-contact team sport, one of two codes of [[Rugby football|rugby football]], the other being [[Rugby league]]. It originated at Rugby School in England in the first half of the 19th century, and in its most common form it is played by two teams of 15 players on a pitch with H-shaped goalposts. Players run with the ball in hand, and points are scored by tries, conversion kicks, penalties and drop goals. In 2023 there were more than 10 million players worldwide, of whom 8.4 million were registered. The sport was amateur until 1995, when formal restrictions on payments to players were removed. The [[Rugby World Cup]], first held in 1987, is contested every four years, and the Six Nations is played annually in [[Europe]].

Iranian Shia cleric and first supreme leader of Iran from 1979 to 1989. He led the [[Iranian Revolution]], which overthrew [[Mohammad Reza Pahlavi]] and transformed Iran into an Islamic republic; his policies became known as Khomeinism. He was named [[Time (magazine)|Time]] magazine's Man of the Year in 1979. He supported the hostage takers in the [[Iran hostage crisis]], and he issued a fatwa calling for the murder of [[Salman Rushdie]] over *The Satanic Verses*. He pursued the overthrow of [[Saddam Hussein]] in the [[Iran–Iraq War]]. His state funeral was attended by up to 10 million people, one fifth of Iran's population at the time. His legacy is contested: some view him as a champion of Islamic revival and independence, while critics point to anti-Western rhetoric, anti-democratic actions and human rights violations, including the 1988 mass executions of political prisoners.
